title: "The module API"
description: "The helpers every graphic module can call, what each one takes and returns, and where to open the full graphics reference."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A graphic is drawn by a small JavaScript module, and every module can call a standard library of helpers for animating values, blending colours, measuring text and following paths. This page is for you if you're writing or changing a module: it names each helper with what it's for, and points you to the full reference. You don't need it to use a graphic.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Help ▸ Graphics Reference"
  where="API.md and API.d.ts in a project's graphics folder"
  tools="graphic_reference"
/>

All of these are already there when your module runs, so there's nothing to import. The examples use the arguments of `render(frame, props, ctx)`: `frame` is the frame being drawn, `props` holds the values set in the inspector, and `ctx` holds the size, frame rate and progress. [Write a graphic module](/graphics/write-a-module/) explains them.

## The graphics reference

Choose **Help ▸ Graphics Reference** to open the whole API in your default Markdown app, with or without a project open. It covers a module's shape, `ctx`, the schema's types, the standard library, fonts, the sandbox, the limits and the worked examples. The menu item is dimmed only if the reference file is missing from the app.

Frame Job also keeps two files beside your modules once a project has a graphics folder:

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `API.md` | The same reference. |
| `API.d.ts` | Type definitions for the whole API, for an editor or an agent working in the folder. |

Frame Job doesn't make a graphics folder only to hold them. Don't edit them, because Frame Job puts its own text back over any change.

An agent reads the same reference with `graphic_reference`, which needs no project open. See [Tools: graphics](/mcp/tools-graphics/).

## Find a helper

| To | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Write the root `<svg>` element | [`svg`](#svg) |
| Move a number from one value to another | [`interpolate`](#interpolate) |
| Shape that movement | [`Easing`](#easing) |
| Move with bounce and settle | [`spring`](#spring) |
| Blend colours | [`interpolateColors`](#interpolatecolors) |
| Get a repeatable random number | [`random`](#random) |
| Add smooth, organic drift | [`noise2D` and `noise3D`](#noise) |
| Measure a path, follow it, or draw it on | [`getLength`, `getPointAtLength` and `evolvePath`](#path-helpers) |
| Measure text | [`measureText`](#measuretext) |
| Break text into lines | [`wrapText`](#wraptext) |
| Size text to a width | [`fitText`](#fittext) |
| Write lines of text as markup | [`textLines`](#textlines) |
| Make a prop safe to put in markup | [`escapeXml`](#escapexml) |
| Group a number's thousands | [`formatNumber`](#formatnumber) |
| Draw a picture from the project | [`asset`](#asset) |

## Start the frame

### `svg()`

`svg(ctx, body, {background})` writes the root element with the right `width`, `height` and `viewBox`, around whatever markup you pass as `body`.

```js
const plain = svg(ctx, `<circle cx="100" cy="100" r="50" fill="#fff"/>`);
const onBlack = svg(ctx, "", { background: "#000000" });
```

`background` is optional and paints the whole frame in a colour. Leave it out and the frame stays clear behind what you draw. `body` goes in exactly as you wrote it, so a prop inside it needs [`escapeXml`](#escapexml).

## Animate values

### `interpolate()`

`interpolate(value, input, output, options)` maps a value through matching ranges. It's the helper most animation starts from.

```js
const x = interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 400], { clamp: true });
const pulse = interpolate(frame, [0, 15, 30], [1, 1.2, 1], { easing: Easing.inOutSine });
```

`input` and `output` need two or more points each, and the same number of them, or the helper throws. Keep `input` ascending.

| Option | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `easing` | A curve from [`Easing`](#easing), applied inside each pair of points. | Straight line |
| `clamp` | With `true`, the result stops at the first and last `output` values. | `false` |
| `extrapolateLeft` | What happens before the first `input` point: `"extend"`, `"clamp"` or `"identity"`. | `"extend"`, or `"clamp"` when `clamp` is `true` |
| `extrapolateRight` | The same after the last `input` point. | `"extend"`, or `"clamp"` when `clamp` is `true` |

Outside `input`, `"extend"` carries on along the end segment, so `interpolate(40, [0, 30], [0, 400])` gives about 533. `"identity"` returns `value` unchanged. Either `extrapolate` option wins over `clamp` on its own side.

### `Easing`

`Easing` holds ready-made curves to pass to `interpolate`. You can also call one directly: each takes `t` from 0 to 1 and is exact at 0 and 1.

- `Easing.linear`
- `Easing.bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)`, which makes a curve of your own
- `in`, `out` and `inOut` of `quad`, `cubic`, `quart`, `expo`, `sine`, `back` and `elastic`, spelled `Easing.inQuad`, `Easing.outCubic`, `Easing.inOutBack` and so on

```js
const eased = Easing.outCubic(0.5);
const custom = Easing.bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1)(0.5);
const y = interpolate(frame, [0, 20], [300, 0], { easing: Easing.outBack, clamp: true });
```

The `back` and `elastic` curves go past the end of their range on the way. `clamp` doesn't stop that, because it only holds the value once `input` runs out.

### `spring()`

`spring()` gives a physical spring from one value to another.

```js
const scale = spring({ frame, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 14 });
const late = spring({ frame: frame - 12, fps: ctx.fps, stiffness: 180, from: 0.5, to: 1 });
```

| Option | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `frame` | The frame to read the spring at. | Needed |
| `fps` | The frame rate. Pass `ctx.fps`. | Needed |
| `stiffness` | How hard the spring pulls towards `to`. | 100 |
| `damping` | How quickly the movement dies away. | 10 |
| `mass` | How heavy the thing moving is. | 1 |
| `from` | Where it starts. | 0 |
| `to` | Where it settles. | 1 |

A spring starts at frame 0 and sits at `from` before that, so `frame - 12` starts it 12 frames late. It overshoots unless it's damped: on the defaults it reaches about 1.16 on its way to 1, and with the default stiffness and mass a `damping` of 20 or more stops the overshoot. The same frame always gives the same value.

### `interpolateColors()`

`interpolateColors(value, input, colors)` blends colours in OKLab, a colour space built so that a blend looks even. It returns `#rrggbb`, or `#rrggbbaa` when any of the colours isn't fully opaque.

```js
const fill = interpolateColors(frame, [0, 60], ["#ff5a36", "#3666ff"]);
const glass = interpolateColors(ctx.progress, [0, 1], ["rgba(255, 255, 255, 0)", "#ffffff"]);
const sky = interpolateColors(ctx.progress, [0, 1], ["hsl(200, 80%, 30%)", "skyblue"]);
```

`input` works as it does in `interpolate`, with two or more points and one colour for each. Outside `input` the result always holds at the end colours.

It takes the same colours a `color` prop takes:

| Form | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `#rgb`, `#rgba`, `#rrggbb`, `#rrggbbaa` | |
| `rgb()`, `rgba()` | Channels 0 to 255 or a percentage, alpha 0 to 1 or a percentage. |
| `hsl()`, `hsla()` | Hue in degrees, saturation and lightness as percentages. |
| A name | Any of the 147 CSS colour names, or `transparent`. |

A value out of range, such as `rgb(300, 0, 0)`, throws rather than being clamped.

## Add variation

### `random()`

`random(seed)` returns a number from 0 up to, but not including, 1. It depends only on the seed, which is a number or a string, so the same seed gives the same number on every frame and in every export.

```js
const jitter = random(`dot-${frame}`) * 10;
const hue = Math.floor(random(42) * 360);
```

Put the frame in the seed for a value that changes, as `jitter` does, and leave it out for one that stays. The seed is read as text, so `42` and `"42"` give the same number.

`Math.random` isn't available in a graphic. Calling it throws "Math.random is not available; use random(seed)".

### Noise

`noise2D(seed, x, y)` and `noise3D(seed, x, y, z)` give simplex noise for organic motion: a value between −1 and 1 that changes smoothly as its inputs do. The seed works as it does for `random`.

```js
const drift = noise2D("wave", frame / 60, 0) * 40;
const wobble = noise3D(7, 0.5, 0.5, ctx.time) * 20;
```

For smooth drift, use `noise3D` with time as the third axis.

## Path helpers

These three take `d`, ordinary SVG path data. Every command works, in its absolute and relative forms: `M L H V C S Q T A Z`.

| Helper | What it returns |
| --- | --- |
| `getLength(d)` | The path's length. Curves and arcs are measured in short straight pieces, so the answer can be a few hundredths of a percent short. |
| `getPointAtLength(d, length)` | `{x, y, angle}`: the point that far along, and the way the path is heading there in degrees, ready for `rotate()`. A `length` outside the path stops at its nearest end. |
| `evolvePath(progress, d)` | `{strokeDasharray, strokeDashoffset}` for a `progress` from 0 to 1. Put both on the `<path>` and it's drawn from its start up to that fraction. |

```js
const d = `M 200 ${ctx.height / 2} C 600 100 1000 900 1400 ${ctx.height / 2}`;
const total = getLength(d);
const tip = getPointAtLength(d, total * ctx.progress);
const dash = evolvePath(ctx.progress, d);
const line = `<path d="${d}" fill="none" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="8"
  stroke-dasharray="${dash.strokeDasharray}" stroke-dashoffset="${dash.strokeDashoffset}"/>
  <circle cx="${tip.x}" cy="${tip.y}" r="12" fill="#ffcc00"/>`;
```

`evolvePath` keeps `progress` between 0 and 1, and a closed outline closes at 1. A path of several pieces, with more than one `M`, draws them all at once, each from its own start and at the same speed, the longest finishing at 1. To draw pieces one after another, give each its own `<path>`.

A path has to start with a move, `M` or `m`. One that can't be read throws, naming where reading stopped, for example `getLength: cannot parse the path at character 6: "X 5 5"`. It's never a silent zero, though an empty `d` measures 0. A number too large to do arithmetic with, such as `1e999`, throws the same error, so you never get `Infinity` or `NaN` back.

Frame Job remembers the paths a graphic measures, so the same `d` costs almost nothing on later calls and frames. It holds up to 32 paths, and about 50,000 characters and measured pieces between them, where a curve is 64 pieces. Past either limit it forgets them all and measures again when asked. With paths that large, take every length and point you need from one before turning to the next.

## Work with text

The text helpers measure with the same fonts the graphic draws with: the ones bundled with Frame Job and any in the project, never the system's. [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/) lists them.

### `measureText()`

`measureText(text, font)` measures text. `font` is an object, and all four text helpers read it the same way:

| Key | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `family` | The font family. | `"Montserrat"` |
| `size` | The size in pixels, above 0. | 16 |
| `weight` | The weight, 1 to 1000. | 400 |
| `style` | `"normal"`, `"italic"` or `"oblique"`. | `"normal"` |
| `letterSpacing` | Extra space between letters. | 0 |
| `xmlSpace` | `"default"` collapses runs of spaces, as SVG draws them. `"preserve"` counts them, as `xml:space="preserve"` draws them. | `"default"` |

It returns `{width, ascent, descent, lineHeight, inkX, inkWidth}`. `width` is the advance, which is where the next word would start. `inkX` and `inkWidth` describe the glyphs actually drawn.

```js
const m = measureText("Hello", { family: "Montserrat", size: 64, weight: 800 });
const boxWidth = m.width + 80;
const gap = measureText("a  b", { family: "sans-serif", size: 48, xmlSpace: "preserve" });
```

A family that isn't installed throws, naming the families that are. Any `xmlSpace` other than those two throws too. Text that's only spaces measures zero either way.

### `wrapText()`

`wrapText(text, maxWidth, font)` breaks text into lines that each fit `maxWidth`, and returns them as a list. A word longer than the width breaks by characters.

```js
const lines = wrapText("A title long enough to need two lines", 600,
  { family: "Source Sans 3", size: 64, weight: 700 });
```

Line breaks in the text count as spaces, so split on them first if you want to keep them.

### `fitText()`

`fitText(text, maxWidth, font, {min, max})` returns the largest whole font size at which the text fits on one line. `min` defaults to 8 and `max` to 400, and the `size` in `font` is ignored.

```js
const size = fitText("BREAKING", ctx.width - 200, { family: "Anton" }, { max: 300 });
```

It never goes outside `min` and `max`, so text too long to fit at `min` still comes back as `min` and runs over. Empty text returns `max`.

### `textLines()`

`textLines(lines, {x, y, lineHeight, anchor, fill, font})` writes a `<text>` element with one `<tspan>` per line.

```js
const font = { family: "Source Sans 3", size: 48, weight: 600 };
const body = textLines(wrapText("Two short lines of text", 400, font),
  { x: 100, y: 200, anchor: "start", fill: "#ffffff", font });
```

| Option | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x`, `y` | Where the first line goes. | 0 |
| `lineHeight` | The distance between lines. | 1.2 × the size |
| `anchor` | `"start"`, `"middle"` or `"end"`. | `"start"` |
| `fill` | The text colour. | Not written |
| `font` | The same `font` object as `measureText`. | |

It does the fiddly parts for you. It quotes the family, leaving a generic such as `sans-serif` bare as it has to be. It escapes each line, so don't pass lines through `escapeXml` first. It also writes `font-style`, `letter-spacing` and `xml:space` to match the font `wrapText` broke the lines with, so what's drawn is what was measured.

## Prepare values

### `escapeXml()`

`escapeXml(s)` escapes `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'`, so a prop is safe to write into markup. Put every prop you write into markup through it. Without it, a title like "Tom & Jerry" stops the frame with an error that starts "the SVG did not parse".

```js
const safe = escapeXml("Tom & Jerry <live>");
```

The exception is text you pass to [`textLines`](#textlines), which escapes it already. Escaping twice puts `&` on screen.

### `formatNumber()`

`formatNumber(n, {decimals, separator})` groups thousands, because a graphic has no `Intl`. `decimals` defaults to 0 and `separator` to a comma.

```js
const label = formatNumber(1234567.891, { decimals: 2 });
const plain = formatNumber(Math.round(interpolate(frame, [0, 60], [0, 5000], { clamp: true })));
```

`label` here is `1,234,567.89`. The number is rounded to `decimals`, a minus sign is kept, and `NaN` or `Infinity` comes back as that word.

## Draw a picture

### `asset()`

`asset(name)` returns the `href` of a file in the project's `graphics/assets/` folder, for an `<image>` element.

```js
const logo = `<image href="${asset("logo.png")}" x="40" y="40" width="200" height="200"/>`;
```

A name that isn't in the folder gives a warning naming the files that are, and the image doesn't draw. [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/) covers adding pictures and how they're named.

## Idioms

The reference ends with six complete modules, each showing a common move. You can copy any of them into a graphic and it works as written. Find them under **Idioms** in **Help ▸ Graphics Reference**.

| Idiom | What it shows | The key line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A slide-in | Text sliding in with `interpolate` and `Easing`. | `interpolate(frame, [0, 18], [-ctx.width / 2, ctx.width / 2], { easing: Easing.outCubic, clamp: true })` |
| A staggered list | Rows springing in one after another. | `spring({ frame: frame - i * 6, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 16 })` |
| A counter | A number counting up. | `formatNumber(Math.round(value)) + props.suffix` |
| Fit and wrap a title | A title sized and wrapped to the frame. | `fitText(props.title, maxWidth * 2, base, { min: 48, max: 220 })`, then `wrapText` and `textLines` |
| A draw-on stroke | A line drawing itself. | `evolvePath(drawn, d)` |
| Follow a path | An arrowhead following a curve. | `getPointAtLength(d, getLength(d) * drawn)`, then `rotate(${tip.angle})` |

All six work out their positions and sizes from `ctx`, so the same module draws at any size. The exception is the `min` and `max` in Fit and wrap a title, which are fixed sizes. A slide-in and A staggered list scale everything by this unit, which also keeps a portrait canvas from drawing too big:

```js
const u = Math.min(ctx.width, ctx.height) / 1080;
```

## Good to know

- A helper that throws stops that frame, and the clip draws the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card) in place of the graphic, or an export stops. The Source section of [the Graphic sub-tab](/graphics/graphic-tab/) shows what the clip's first frame reported, with its line and column.
- `import` isn't available. A module that tries it stops with an error ending "imports are not available in a graphic; the standard library is global".

## Related

- [Write a graphic module](/graphics/write-a-module/)
- [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/)
- [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/)
- [Graphics with an agent](/graphics/agents-and-graphics/)
- [Tools: graphics](/mcp/tools-graphics/)

title: What a call answers
description: How to read a tool's answer. A landed edit, a call that changed nothing, a refusal, an error, what a cloud tool says with no key, and which tools never touch the network.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A call tells you what happened in its answer, in words a model can act on. An edit lands, changes nothing, is refused, or is an error, and each reads differently.

<AtAGlance
  tools={['transcribe', 'transcribe_for_fillers', 'get_media_analysis', 'get_transcript', 'get_timeline_transcript', 'detect_fillers', 'detect_silence', 'split_at_shots', 'analyze_cutout']}
  needs="Your AssemblyAI key, only for a tool that sends to AssemblyAI."
/>

## Answers come back as tool results

Every answer comes back as the tool's result, so a model can read it and correct itself. A refused or invalid call is an ordinary tool result with `isError: true`, and its text is the message. It isn't a transport or JSON-RPC error. A call that changed nothing is marked the same way, and its message says the project is already in that state.

JSON-RPC errors are for the protocol itself. An MCP method the server doesn't know gets "method not found", and a `tools/call` with no tool name is an error too. A tool name that doesn't exist is an ordinary result: "Unknown tool: *name*".

| The answer | `isError` | Undo step | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [A landed edit](#a-landed-edit) | false | One | Read the ids and carry on |
| [No change](#a-no-change-answer) | true | None | Nothing. The project already says that. |
| [A refusal](#a-refusal) | true | None | Act on the reason, then call again |
| [An error](#an-error) | true | None | Fix the argument it names, then call again |

## A landed edit

An edit that landed answers `ok: true`, the ids it created, anything the tool adds of its own, and a short `project` summary. A model doesn't need to read the whole project back to see what it did.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "new_clips": [42],
  "project": {
    "name": "Interview",
    "path": "/Volumes/Work/Interview.framejob",
    "width": 1920,
    "height": 1080,
    "fps": [30, 1],
    "duration": 1800000,
    "playhead": 600000,
    "tracks": 3,
    "clips": 7,
    "markers": 2,
    "media": 4,
    "selection": [],
    "unsaved_changes": true
  }
}
```

The ids appear only when the edit created something:

| Key | What it lists |
| --- | --- |
| `new_clips` | Clips the edit created, inside any nest too |
| `new_tracks` | Tracks the edit created, inside any nest too |
| `new_markers` | Markers the edit created |
| `new_media` | Media the edit added |
| `new_actions` | Actions, from the tools that add them, such as `add_action` |

The summary holds:

| Key | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `name`, `path` | The project's name and its path, which is `null` for a project with no file yet |
| `width`, `height`, `fps` | The canvas. `fps` is `[numerator, denominator]`. |
| `duration`, `playhead` | Both in [ticks](/mcp/units-and-ids/#times-in-ticks) |
| `tracks`, `clips`, `markers`, `media` | How many of each, counted on the top-level timeline |
| `selection` | The ids of the selected clips |
| `unsaved_changes` | Whether the project has changes to save |
| `missing_media` | The ids of media whose file is gone. It only appears when there are some, and `relink_media` points one at its new place. |

An edit made inside a nest also answers `scope`, the nest it landed in. See [Editing inside a nest](/mcp/nests/). A speed edit that takes a clip past ×12 adds `audio_left_out` and `audio_note`.

Every edit is exactly [one undo step](/mcp/tool-calls/#one-call-one-undo-step), however many clips it touched.

## A no-change answer

> Video Properties made no change: the project is already in that state.

This means nothing was wrong. The project already says what you asked, so no undo step was made and it's safe to retry. The message opens with the name the step would have had in the **Edit** menu.

## A refusal

> Remove Track was refused at remove_track: track 3 still holds clip 12; pass with_clips: true to remove the track and its clips

A rule declined the edit. The message reads *step* was refused at *edit*: *reason*. The reason names what you can act on:

- a track that's locked
- the clips still using a media file
- how far two clips would overlap
- the argument that lets the call through, such as `with_clips: true` or `ripple: true`

The project is untouched and no undo step is made, so you can fix the cause and call again.

## An error

An argument Frame Job can't use is an error, and it's marked and treated like a refusal: nothing changes and no undo step is made. The message names the argument.

| What went wrong | Example |
| --- | --- |
| An id nothing has | `No clip has id 17. get_project lists the clips.` |
| A required argument left out | `Missing required argument: clip (an id)` |
| An argument the tool doesn't take | `trim_start does not take speed. It takes alone, clip, to, project and scope.` |
| A bad key or value in a patch | `unknown key "gate.knee" in an audio patch` |

A message starting "internal error:" means something went wrong inside Frame Job. The project is unchanged.

[Patches](/mcp/patches/#patch-refusals-name-the-path) has more of these, and [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/) gives the rules they come from.

## Keyed tools with no key

Two tools can send to AssemblyAI, and both use the key and region saved in **Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Transcription**. A person has to set the key first, because [no tool can set or read it](/captions/assemblyai-key/#only-a-person-sets-the-key).

A tool needs the key only at the moment it would send. Without one it refuses there, before anything is uploaded:

> No AssemblyAI API key is set. Set one in Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Transcription.

| Tool | Needs the key | Doesn't need the key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `transcribe` | With `engine: "assemblyai"` when a file has no usable transcript, or with `refresh: true` | The default `apple` engine, or when every file already has a current transcript in the project |
| `transcribe_for_fillers` | When it has to upload the file | When the file already has a transcript made with filler words |

No tool needs an Anthropic key. That key is only for the [Assistant](/assistant/set-up/) inside Frame Job.

## Tools that never reach the network

These tools read what's on your Mac. They never make a network request, upload anything or need a key, whatever you pass them.

| Tool | What it reads |
| --- | --- |
| `get_media_analysis` | Analysis made on your Mac and kept in the project's cache |
| `split_at_shots` | The same analysis, for shot changes |
| `analyze_cutout` | Masks made on your Mac |
| `detect_silence` | The cached waveform and voice detection |
| `detect_fillers` | An AssemblyAI transcript already in the project. A file with no such transcript is listed under `needs_transcript`. |
| `get_transcript` | A cached transcript, or your Mac's own speech recogniser |
| `get_timeline_transcript` | A cached transcript, or your Mac's own speech recogniser |

## Related

- [How tool calls behave](/mcp/tool-calls/)
- [Patches](/mcp/patches/)
- [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/)
- [Tools: captions and transcripts](/mcp/tools-captions/)
- [Your AssemblyAI key](/captions/assemblyai-key/)
- [When an edit is refused](/getting-started/refused-edits/)

title: "Check the picture: render_frame"
description: "Render one frame of the finished timeline so an agent can see its work, choose the file it writes, draw grade and HDR variants, and measure the scopes."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

`render_frame` draws one frame of the finished timeline, so an agent can see what it has done. It's drawn the same way an export draws it, so the picture is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Save Frame…"
  keys="⌥⌘E"
  tools="render_frame"
/>

## Render a frame

With no arguments it draws the frame under the playhead at the canvas's size and writes a PNG to a temporary file.

```json
{ "t": 1200000, "path": "/tmp/shot.png", "max_width": 960 }
```

The picture comes back two ways: as an image the model can see, and as a file on disk. The text beside it says what was drawn and ends by naming the file:

```
Frame at 1200000 ticks of a 1920×1080 px canvas, rendered at 960×540 px. Written to /tmp/shot.png.
```

It uses the same writer as [**File ▸ Save Frame…**](/export/save-frame/), so a PNG from either one is identical, byte for byte.

With a [nest](/mcp/nests/) open, it draws that nest at its own size, from its own zero, without the nest clip's position, scale or opacity. It takes no `scope`, so open the nest with [`set_scope`](/mcp/tools-view-state/#set_scope) to look inside.

| Argument | Type | Required | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`t`](#t) | integer | No | The moment to render, in ticks. | The playhead |
| [`path`](#path) | string | No | Where to write the file. | A temporary file |
18:| A nest | With a [nest](/editing/nests/) open, these are off: **New Project from Range…**, **Make Vertical Version…**, **Rename Graphic…**, **Add Marker**, **Next Marker**, **Previous Marker**, **Insert ▸ Adjustment Clip** and **Text Behind Subject**. Leave the nest with <kbd>⌘↑</kbd>. |
92:An agent's `import_media` reports these reasons too.
98:When a project opens with files missing, Frame Job offers the **Missing media** sheet once. Choose **Locate…** for a file, then **Relink**. Frame Job also looks in that file's folder for the other missing files by name, so a shoot moved as one folder is usually found in one go. To relink a file later, use **Relink…** on its row in the Media tab. An agent uses `relink_media`.
124:An export that fails says why and leaves no finished file. An agent reads the same reason from `export_status`.
134:| "The export was not started: the graphic…" or "The export was stopped at frame *N* of the graphic…" | Frame Job won't export a graphic that can't draw itself. Fix its [module](/graphics/edit-a-module/) and export again. |
159:An agent can't set a key, so a person has to. See [AI features and your own keys](/getting-started/ai-and-your-keys/).
170:An agent's `record_screen` never asks for a permission, so a person has to grant it first. See [Recording permissions](/recording/permissions/).
172:## An agent can't reach Frame Job
174:Only programs running as you can connect, through the `framejob-mcp` helper inside the app.
178:| The client can't start the helper after you moved Frame Job | In the **MCP** section of [Settings](/reference/settings/#mcp), press **Copy MCP Command** and register the new path. The path is the one you opened Settings from, and it doesn't follow the app. |
179:| "framejob-mcp is missing from this copy of Frame Job." | The helper isn't in this copy. Use a complete copy of the app. |
182:See [Connect a client](/mcp/connect-a-client/).

title: "The module API"
description: "The helpers every graphic module can call, what each one takes and returns, and where to open the full graphics reference."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A graphic is drawn by a small JavaScript module, and every module can call a standard library of helpers for animating values, blending colours, measuring text and following paths. This page is for you if you're writing or changing a module: it names each helper with what it's for, and points you to the full reference. You don't need it to use a graphic.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Help ▸ Graphics Reference"
  where="API.md and API.d.ts in a project's graphics folder"
  tools="graphic_reference"
/>

All of these are already there when your module runs, so there's nothing to import. The examples use the arguments of `render(frame, props, ctx)`: `frame` is the frame being drawn, `props` holds the values set in the inspector, and `ctx` holds the size, frame rate and progress. [Write a graphic module](/graphics/write-a-module/) explains them.

## The graphics reference

Choose **Help ▸ Graphics Reference** to open the whole API in your default Markdown app, with or without a project open. It covers a module's shape, `ctx`, the schema's types, the standard library, fonts, the sandbox, the limits and the worked examples. The menu item is dimmed only if the reference file is missing from the app.

Frame Job also keeps two files beside your modules once a project has a graphics folder:

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `API.md` | The same reference. |
| `API.d.ts` | Type definitions for the whole API, for an editor or an agent working in the folder. |

Frame Job doesn't make a graphics folder only to hold them. Don't edit them, because Frame Job puts its own text back over any change.

An agent reads the same reference with `graphic_reference`, which needs no project open. See [Tools: graphics](/mcp/tools-graphics/).

## Find a helper

| To | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Write the root `<svg>` element | [`svg`](#svg) |
| Move a number from one value to another | [`interpolate`](#interpolate) |
| Shape that movement | [`Easing`](#easing) |
| Move with bounce and settle | [`spring`](#spring) |
| Blend colours | [`interpolateColors`](#interpolatecolors) |
| Get a repeatable random number | [`random`](#random) |
| Add smooth, organic drift | [`noise2D` and `noise3D`](#noise) |
| Measure a path, follow it, or draw it on | [`getLength`, `getPointAtLength` and `evolvePath`](#path-helpers) |
| Measure text | [`measureText`](#measuretext) |
| Break text into lines | [`wrapText`](#wraptext) |
| Size text to a width | [`fitText`](#fittext) |
| Write lines of text as markup | [`textLines`](#textlines) |
| Make a prop safe to put in markup | [`escapeXml`](#escapexml) |
| Group a number's thousands | [`formatNumber`](#formatnumber) |
| Draw a picture from the project | [`asset`](#asset) |

## Start the frame

### `svg()`

`svg(ctx, body, {background})` writes the root element with the right `width`, `height` and `viewBox`, around whatever markup you pass as `body`.

```js
const plain = svg(ctx, `<circle cx="100" cy="100" r="50" fill="#fff"/>`);
const onBlack = svg(ctx, "", { background: "#000000" });
```

`background` is optional and paints the whole frame in a colour. Leave it out and the frame stays clear behind what you draw. `body` goes in exactly as you wrote it, so a prop inside it needs [`escapeXml`](#escapexml).

## Animate values

### `interpolate()`

`interpolate(value, input, output, options)` maps a value through matching ranges. It's the helper most animation starts from.

```js
const x = interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 400], { clamp: true });
const pulse = interpolate(frame, [0, 15, 30], [1, 1.2, 1], { easing: Easing.inOutSine });
```

`input` and `output` need two or more points each, and the same number of them, or the helper throws. Keep `input` ascending.

| Option | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `easing` | A curve from [`Easing`](#easing), applied inside each pair of points. | Straight line |
| `clamp` | With `true`, the result stops at the first and last `output` values. | `false` |
| `extrapolateLeft` | What happens before the first `input` point: `"extend"`, `"clamp"` or `"identity"`. | `"extend"`, or `"clamp"` when `clamp` is `true` |
| `extrapolateRight` | The same after the last `input` point. | `"extend"`, or `"clamp"` when `clamp` is `true` |

Outside `input`, `"extend"` carries on along the end segment, so `interpolate(40, [0, 30], [0, 400])` gives about 533. `"identity"` returns `value` unchanged. Either `extrapolate` option wins over `clamp` on its own side.

### `Easing`

`Easing` holds ready-made curves to pass to `interpolate`. You can also call one directly: each takes `t` from 0 to 1 and is exact at 0 and 1.

- `Easing.linear`
- `Easing.bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)`, which makes a curve of your own
- `in`, `out` and `inOut` of `quad`, `cubic`, `quart`, `expo`, `sine`, `back` and `elastic`, spelled `Easing.inQuad`, `Easing.outCubic`, `Easing.inOutBack` and so on

```js
const eased = Easing.outCubic(0.5);
const custom = Easing.bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1)(0.5);
const y = interpolate(frame, [0, 20], [300, 0], { easing: Easing.outBack, clamp: true });
```

The `back` and `elastic` curves go past the end of their range on the way. `clamp` doesn't stop that, because it only holds the value once `input` runs out.

### `spring()`

`spring()` gives a physical spring from one value to another.

```js
const scale = spring({ frame, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 14 });
const late = spring({ frame: frame - 12, fps: ctx.fps, stiffness: 180, from: 0.5, to: 1 });
```

| Option | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `frame` | The frame to read the spring at. | Needed |
| `fps` | The frame rate. Pass `ctx.fps`. | Needed |
| `stiffness` | How hard the spring pulls towards `to`. | 100 |
| `damping` | How quickly the movement dies away. | 10 |
| `mass` | How heavy the thing moving is. | 1 |
| `from` | Where it starts. | 0 |
| `to` | Where it settles. | 1 |

A spring starts at frame 0 and sits at `from` before that, so `frame - 12` starts it 12 frames late. It overshoots unless it's damped: on the defaults it reaches about 1.16 on its way to 1, and with the default stiffness and mass a `damping` of 20 or more stops the overshoot. The same frame always gives the same value.

### `interpolateColors()`

`interpolateColors(value, input, colors)` blends colours in OKLab, a colour space built so that a blend looks even. It returns `#rrggbb`, or `#rrggbbaa` when any of the colours isn't fully opaque.

```js
const fill = interpolateColors(frame, [0, 60], ["#ff5a36", "#3666ff"]);
const glass = interpolateColors(ctx.progress, [0, 1], ["rgba(255, 255, 255, 0)", "#ffffff"]);
const sky = interpolateColors(ctx.progress, [0, 1], ["hsl(200, 80%, 30%)", "skyblue"]);
```

`input` works as it does in `interpolate`, with two or more points and one colour for each. Outside `input` the result always holds at the end colours.

It takes the same colours a `color` prop takes:

| Form | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `#rgb`, `#rgba`, `#rrggbb`, `#rrggbbaa` | |
| `rgb()`, `rgba()` | Channels 0 to 255 or a percentage, alpha 0 to 1 or a percentage. |
| `hsl()`, `hsla()` | Hue in degrees, saturation and lightness as percentages. |
| A name | Any of the 147 CSS colour names, or `transparent`. |

A value out of range, such as `rgb(300, 0, 0)`, throws rather than being clamped.

## Add variation

### `random()`

`random(seed)` returns a number from 0 up to, but not including, 1. It depends only on the seed, which is a number or a string, so the same seed gives the same number on every frame and in every export.

```js
const jitter = random(`dot-${frame}`) * 10;
const hue = Math.floor(random(42) * 360);
```

Put the frame in the seed for a value that changes, as `jitter` does, and leave it out for one that stays. The seed is read as text, so `42` and `"42"` give the same number.

`Math.random` isn't available in a graphic. Calling it throws "Math.random is not available; use random(seed)".

### Noise

`noise2D(seed, x, y)` and `noise3D(seed, x, y, z)` give simplex noise for organic motion: a value between −1 and 1 that changes smoothly as its inputs do. The seed works as it does for `random`.

```js
const drift = noise2D("wave", frame / 60, 0) * 40;
const wobble = noise3D(7, 0.5, 0.5, ctx.time) * 20;
```

For smooth drift, use `noise3D` with time as the third axis.

## Path helpers

These three take `d`, ordinary SVG path data. Every command works, in its absolute and relative forms: `M L H V C S Q T A Z`.

| Helper | What it returns |
| --- | --- |
| `getLength(d)` | The path's length. Curves and arcs are measured in short straight pieces, so the answer can be a few hundredths of a percent short. |
| `getPointAtLength(d, length)` | `{x, y, angle}`: the point that far along, and the way the path is heading there in degrees, ready for `rotate()`. A `length` outside the path stops at its nearest end. |
| `evolvePath(progress, d)` | `{strokeDasharray, strokeDashoffset}` for a `progress` from 0 to 1. Put both on the `<path>` and it's drawn from its start up to that fraction. |

```js
const d = `M 200 ${ctx.height / 2} C 600 100 1000 900 1400 ${ctx.height / 2}`;
const total = getLength(d);
const tip = getPointAtLength(d, total * ctx.progress);
const dash = evolvePath(ctx.progress, d);
const line = `<path d="${d}" fill="none" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="8"
  stroke-dasharray="${dash.strokeDasharray}" stroke-dashoffset="${dash.strokeDashoffset}"/>
  <circle cx="${tip.x}" cy="${tip.y}" r="12" fill="#ffcc00"/>`;
```

`evolvePath` keeps `progress` between 0 and 1, and a closed outline closes at 1. A path of several pieces, with more than one `M`, draws them all at once, each from its own start and at the same speed, the longest finishing at 1. To draw pieces one after another, give each its own `<path>`.

A path has to start with a move, `M` or `m`. One that can't be read throws, naming where reading stopped, for example `getLength: cannot parse the path at character 6: "X 5 5"`. It's never a silent zero, though an empty `d` measures 0. A number too large to do arithmetic with, such as `1e999`, throws the same error, so you never get `Infinity` or `NaN` back.

Frame Job remembers the paths a graphic measures, so the same `d` costs almost nothing on later calls and frames. It holds up to 32 paths, and about 50,000 characters and measured pieces between them, where a curve is 64 pieces. Past either limit it forgets them all and measures again when asked. With paths that large, take every length and point you need from one before turning to the next.

## Work with text

The text helpers measure with the same fonts the graphic draws with: the ones bundled with Frame Job and any in the project, never the system's. [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/) lists them.

### `measureText()`

`measureText(text, font)` measures text. `font` is an object, and all four text helpers read it the same way:

| Key | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `family` | The font family. | `"Montserrat"` |
| `size` | The size in pixels, above 0. | 16 |
| `weight` | The weight, 1 to 1000. | 400 |
| `style` | `"normal"`, `"italic"` or `"oblique"`. | `"normal"` |
| `letterSpacing` | Extra space between letters. | 0 |
| `xmlSpace` | `"default"` collapses runs of spaces, as SVG draws them. `"preserve"` counts them, as `xml:space="preserve"` draws them. | `"default"` |

It returns `{width, ascent, descent, lineHeight, inkX, inkWidth}`. `width` is the advance, which is where the next word would start. `inkX` and `inkWidth` describe the glyphs actually drawn.

```js
const m = measureText("Hello", { family: "Montserrat", size: 64, weight: 800 });
const boxWidth = m.width + 80;
const gap = measureText("a  b", { family: "sans-serif", size: 48, xmlSpace: "preserve" });
```

A family that isn't installed throws, naming the families that are. Any `xmlSpace` other than those two throws too. Text that's only spaces measures zero either way.

### `wrapText()`

`wrapText(text, maxWidth, font)` breaks text into lines that each fit `maxWidth`, and returns them as a list. A word longer than the width breaks by characters.

```js
const lines = wrapText("A title long enough to need two lines", 600,
  { family: "Source Sans 3", size: 64, weight: 700 });
```

Line breaks in the text count as spaces, so split on them first if you want to keep them.

### `fitText()`

`fitText(text, maxWidth, font, {min, max})` returns the largest whole font size at which the text fits on one line. `min` defaults to 8 and `max` to 400, and the `size` in `font` is ignored.

```js
const size = fitText("BREAKING", ctx.width - 200, { family: "Anton" }, { max: 300 });
```

It never goes outside `min` and `max`, so text too long to fit at `min` still comes back as `min` and runs over. Empty text returns `max`.

### `textLines()`

`textLines(lines, {x, y, lineHeight, anchor, fill, font})` writes a `<text>` element with one `<tspan>` per line.

```js
const font = { family: "Source Sans 3", size: 48, weight: 600 };
const body = textLines(wrapText("Two short lines of text", 400, font),
  { x: 100, y: 200, anchor: "start", fill: "#ffffff", font });
```

| Option | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x`, `y` | Where the first line goes. | 0 |
| `lineHeight` | The distance between lines. | 1.2 × the size |
| `anchor` | `"start"`, `"middle"` or `"end"`. | `"start"` |
| `fill` | The text colour. | Not written |
| `font` | The same `font` object as `measureText`. | |

It does the fiddly parts for you. It quotes the family, leaving a generic such as `sans-serif` bare as it has to be. It escapes each line, so don't pass lines through `escapeXml` first. It also writes `font-style`, `letter-spacing` and `xml:space` to match the font `wrapText` broke the lines with, so what's drawn is what was measured.

## Prepare values

### `escapeXml()`

`escapeXml(s)` escapes `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'`, so a prop is safe to write into markup. Put every prop you write into markup through it. Without it, a title like "Tom & Jerry" stops the frame with an error that starts "the SVG did not parse".

```js
const safe = escapeXml("Tom & Jerry <live>");
```

The exception is text you pass to [`textLines`](#textlines), which escapes it already. Escaping twice puts `&` on screen.

### `formatNumber()`

`formatNumber(n, {decimals, separator})` groups thousands, because a graphic has no `Intl`. `decimals` defaults to 0 and `separator` to a comma.

```js
const label = formatNumber(1234567.891, { decimals: 2 });
const plain = formatNumber(Math.round(interpolate(frame, [0, 60], [0, 5000], { clamp: true })));
```

`label` here is `1,234,567.89`. The number is rounded to `decimals`, a minus sign is kept, and `NaN` or `Infinity` comes back as that word.

## Draw a picture

### `asset()`

`asset(name)` returns the `href` of a file in the project's `graphics/assets/` folder, for an `<image>` element.

```js
const logo = `<image href="${asset("logo.png")}" x="40" y="40" width="200" height="200"/>`;
```

A name that isn't in the folder gives a warning naming the files that are, and the image doesn't draw. [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/) covers adding pictures and how they're named.

## Idioms

The reference ends with six complete modules, each showing a common move. You can copy any of them into a graphic and it works as written. Find them under **Idioms** in **Help ▸ Graphics Reference**.

| Idiom | What it shows | The key line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A slide-in | Text sliding in with `interpolate` and `Easing`. | `interpolate(frame, [0, 18], [-ctx.width / 2, ctx.width / 2], { easing: Easing.outCubic, clamp: true })` |
| A staggered list | Rows springing in one after another. | `spring({ frame: frame - i * 6, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 16 })` |
| A counter | A number counting up. | `formatNumber(Math.round(value)) + props.suffix` |
| Fit and wrap a title | A title sized and wrapped to the frame. | `fitText(props.title, maxWidth * 2, base, { min: 48, max: 220 })`, then `wrapText` and `textLines` |
| A draw-on stroke | A line drawing itself. | `evolvePath(drawn, d)` |
| Follow a path | An arrowhead following a curve. | `getPointAtLength(d, getLength(d) * drawn)`, then `rotate(${tip.angle})` |

All six work out their positions and sizes from `ctx`, so the same module draws at any size. The exception is the `min` and `max` in Fit and wrap a title, which are fixed sizes. A slide-in and A staggered list scale everything by this unit, which also keeps a portrait canvas from drawing too big:

```js
const u = Math.min(ctx.width, ctx.height) / 1080;
```

## Good to know

- A helper that throws stops that frame, and the clip draws the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card) in place of the graphic, or an export stops. The Source section of [the Graphic sub-tab](/graphics/graphic-tab/) shows what the clip's first frame reported, with its line and column.
- `import` isn't available. A module that tries it stops with an error ending "imports are not available in a graphic; the standard library is global".

title: What a call answers
description: How to read a tool's answer. A landed edit, a call that changed nothing, a refusal, an error, what a cloud tool says with no key, and which tools never touch the network.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A call tells you what happened in its answer, in words a model can act on. An edit lands, changes nothing, is refused, or is an error, and each reads differently.

<AtAGlance
  tools={['transcribe', 'transcribe_for_fillers', 'get_media_analysis', 'get_transcript', 'get_timeline_transcript', 'detect_fillers', 'detect_silence', 'split_at_shots', 'analyze_cutout']}
  needs="Your AssemblyAI key, only for a tool that sends to AssemblyAI."
/>

## Answers come back as tool results

Every answer comes back as the tool's result, so a model can read it and correct itself. A refused or invalid call is an ordinary tool result with `isError: true`, and its text is the message. It isn't a transport or JSON-RPC error. A call that changed nothing is marked the same way, and its message says the project is already in that state.

JSON-RPC errors are for the protocol itself. An MCP method the server doesn't know gets "method not found", and a `tools/call` with no tool name is an error too. A tool name that doesn't exist is an ordinary result: "Unknown tool: *name*".

| The answer | `isError` | Undo step | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [A landed edit](#a-landed-edit) | false | One | Read the ids and carry on |
| [No change](#a-no-change-answer) | true | None | Nothing. The project already says that. |
| [A refusal](#a-refusal) | true | None | Act on the reason, then call again |
| [An error](#an-error) | true | None | Fix the argument it names, then call again |

## A landed edit

An edit that landed answers `ok: true`, the ids it created, anything the tool adds of its own, and a short `project` summary. A model doesn't need to read the whole project back to see what it did.

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "new_clips": [42],
  "project": {
    "name": "Interview",
    "path": "/Volumes/Work/Interview.framejob",
    "width": 1920,
    "height": 1080,
    "fps": [30, 1],
    "duration": 1800000,
    "playhead": 600000,
    "tracks": 3,
    "clips": 7,
    "markers": 2,
    "media": 4,
    "selection": [],
    "unsaved_changes": true
  }
}
```

The ids appear only when the edit created something:

| Key | What it lists |
| --- | --- |
| `new_clips` | Clips the edit created, inside any nest too |
| `new_tracks` | Tracks the edit created, inside any nest too |
| `new_markers` | Markers the edit created |
| `new_media` | Media the edit added |
| `new_actions` | Actions, from the tools that add them, such as `add_action` |

The summary holds:

| Key | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `name`, `path` | The project's name and its path, which is `null` for a project with no file yet |
| `width`, `height`, `fps` | The canvas. `fps` is `[numerator, denominator]`. |
| `duration`, `playhead` | Both in [ticks](/mcp/units-and-ids/#times-in-ticks) |
| `tracks`, `clips`, `markers`, `media` | How many of each, counted on the top-level timeline |
| `selection` | The ids of the selected clips |
| `unsaved_changes` | Whether the project has changes to save |
| `missing_media` | The ids of media whose file is gone. It only appears when there are some, and `relink_media` points one at its new place. |

An edit made inside a nest also answers `scope`, the nest it landed in. See [Editing inside a nest](/mcp/nests/). A speed edit that takes a clip past ×12 adds `audio_left_out` and `audio_note`.

Every edit is exactly [one undo step](/mcp/tool-calls/#one-call-one-undo-step), however many clips it touched.

## A no-change answer

> Video Properties made no change: the project is already in that state.

This means nothing was wrong. The project already says what you asked, so no undo step was made and it's safe to retry. The message opens with the name the step would have had in the **Edit** menu.

## A refusal

> Remove Track was refused at remove_track: track 3 still holds clip 12; pass with_clips: true to remove the track and its clips

A rule declined the edit. The message reads *step* was refused at *edit*: *reason*. The reason names what you can act on:

- a track that's locked
- the clips still using a media file
- how far two clips would overlap
- the argument that lets the call through, such as `with_clips: true` or `ripple: true`

The project is untouched and no undo step is made, so you can fix the cause and call again.

## An error

An argument Frame Job can't use is an error, and it's marked and treated like a refusal: nothing changes and no undo step is made. The message names the argument.

| What went wrong | Example |
| --- | --- |
| An id nothing has | `No clip has id 17. get_project lists the clips.` |
| A required argument left out | `Missing required argument: clip (an id)` |
| An argument the tool doesn't take | `trim_start does not take speed. It takes alone, clip, to, project and scope.` |
| A bad key or value in a patch | `unknown key "gate.knee" in an audio patch` |

A message starting "internal error:" means something went wrong inside Frame Job. The project is unchanged.

[Patches](/mcp/patches/#patch-refusals-name-the-path) has more of these, and [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/) gives the rules they come from.

## Keyed tools with no key

Two tools can send to AssemblyAI, and both use the key and region saved in **Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Transcription**. A person has to set the key first, because [no tool can set or read it](/captions/assemblyai-key/#only-a-person-sets-the-key).

A tool needs the key only at the moment it would send. Without one it refuses there, before anything is uploaded:

> No AssemblyAI API key is set. Set one in Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Transcription.

| Tool | Needs the key | Doesn't need the key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `transcribe` | With `engine: "assemblyai"` when a file has no usable transcript, or with `refresh: true` | The default `apple` engine, or when every file already has a current transcript in the project |
| `transcribe_for_fillers` | When it has to upload the file | When the file already has a transcript made with filler words |

No tool needs an Anthropic key. That key is only for the [Assistant](/assistant/set-up/) inside Frame Job.

## Tools that never reach the network

These tools read what's on your Mac. They never make a network request, upload anything or need a key, whatever you pass them.

| Tool | What it reads |
| --- | --- |
| `get_media_analysis` | Analysis made on your Mac and kept in the project's cache |
| `split_at_shots` | The same analysis, for shot changes |
| `analyze_cutout` | Masks made on your Mac |
| `detect_silence` | The cached waveform and voice detection |
| `detect_fillers` | An AssemblyAI transcript already in the project. A file with no such transcript is listed under `needs_transcript`. |
| `get_transcript` | A cached transcript, or your Mac's own speech recogniser |
| `get_timeline_transcript` | A cached transcript, or your Mac's own speech recogniser |

## Related

title: "Check the picture: render_frame"
description: "Render one frame of the finished timeline so an agent can see its work, choose the file it writes, draw grade and HDR variants, and measure the scopes."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

`render_frame` draws one frame of the finished timeline, so an agent can see what it has done. It's drawn the same way an export draws it, so the picture is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Save Frame…"
  keys="⌥⌘E"
  tools="render_frame"
/>

## Render a frame

With no arguments it draws the frame under the playhead at the canvas's size and writes a PNG to a temporary file.

```json
{ "t": 1200000, "path": "/tmp/shot.png", "max_width": 960 }
```

The picture comes back two ways: as an image the model can see, and as a file on disk. The text beside it says what was drawn and ends by naming the file:

```
Frame at 1200000 ticks of a 1920×1080 px canvas, rendered at 960×540 px. Written to /tmp/shot.png.
```

It uses the same writer as [**File ▸ Save Frame…**](/export/save-frame/), so a PNG from either one is identical, byte for byte.

With a [nest](/mcp/nests/) open, it draws that nest at its own size, from its own zero, without the nest clip's position, scale or opacity. It takes no `scope`, so open the nest with [`set_scope`](/mcp/tools-view-state/#set_scope) to look inside.

| Argument | Type | Required | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`t`](#t) | integer | No | The moment to render, in ticks. | The playhead |
| [`path`](#path) | string | No | Where to write the file. | A temporary file |

- **Screen Recording** is at **System Settings ▸ Privacy & Security ▸ Screen & System Audio Recording**. Once it's on, relaunch Frame Job, then press Record again. Later presses without it open that pane.
- **Microphone**, **Camera** and **Input Monitoring** are asked for only when the recording needs them.

| "framejob-mcp is missing from this copy of Frame Job." | The helper isn't in this copy. Use a complete copy of the app. |
| "Frame Job did not answer at…" | Frame Job launched but wasn't ready within 60 seconds. Later calls in that client session don't launch another copy, so quit the stray copy and try again. |

title: AI features and your own keys
description: Which features need nothing, which use an on-device model, which need your own Anthropic or AssemblyAI key, and what ever leaves your Mac.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Most of Frame Job needs no key and no network. The few features that send your words or audio to a cloud model run on your own API keys, so you decide what's used and you pay the provider directly.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Frame Job ▸ Settings…"
  keys="⌘,"
  where={['Settings ▸ Assistant', 'Settings ▸ Transcription']}
  tools={['transcribe', 'transcribe_for_fillers']}
  needs="Your own Anthropic or AssemblyAI key, only for the features that send to them."
/>

## Your own keys

There's no Frame Job account and no relay in between. There are two keys in all, and each provider bills your account directly.

| Key | Turns on | Saved in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anthropic | The Assistant | [Settings ▸ Assistant](/assistant/set-up/) |
| AssemblyAI | Cloud captions and Remove Filler Words | [Settings ▸ Transcription](/captions/assemblyai-key/) |

Frame Job shows its own estimate of what each Assistant turn and each month costs. See [What it costs](/assistant/cost/). The provider's bill is the real figure.

With no key set, Settings says "No API key is set." in its ordinary muted colour. That only means there's no key yet, and it isn't an error.

## What needs what

Anything that sends your words or audio to a language or cloud model needs your own key. Everything that runs on your Mac needs none.

| What it takes | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Nothing | Editing, colour, graphics, recording, export and Split at Shot Changes |
| An on-device model, with no key and no upload | **Generate Captions** with **On this Mac**, Remove Silences' voice analysis, Enhance Voice and Voice Isolation, Remove Background, Follow Subject, Make Vertical Version and Switch by Speaker |
| Your AssemblyAI key | The **AssemblyAI** engine of **File ▸ Generate Captions…**, and **Clip ▸ Remove Filler Words…** with its **Transcribe** buttons |
| Your Anthropic key | The Assistant |

Filler removal works only through AssemblyAI. There's no on-device version.

Without your Anthropic key, **View ▸ Assistant** still opens the tab, which says how to add the key.

Work you've already paid for keeps working with no key:

- **Generate** isn't greyed when every file is already transcribed.
- **Remove Filler Words…** stays on while a file it would work on has a current transcript made with filler words.

An on-device language that isn't installed yet shows a **Download** row in the [Generate Captions](/captions/generate-captions/) sheet.

## Greyed commands

A command that needs a key you haven't set is greyed rather than hidden, and it says which key and where to set it.

A greyed menu item's title gains the key's name, as in **Remove Filler Words… (needs your AssemblyAI key)**. Rest the pointer on a greyed command or button and it reads:

> No AssemblyAI API key is set. Set one in Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Transcription.

For the Assistant it's the same sentence with Anthropic and Assistant. The Assistant tab itself reads "Add your Anthropic API key in Settings to use the assistant." with an **Open Settings…** button.

An agent's tool stops with the same sentence, at the point it would send. See [Transcripts for filler words](/cleanup/filler-transcripts/) for what still works without a key.

## Saving a key takes effect at once

Saving or removing a key updates open sheets and menu items straight away. An open Generate Captions sheet turns **Generate** back on with the sheet still up, and there's nothing to reopen or relaunch.

## What stays on this Mac

For what you get from each, see [Start a project](/projects/start-a-project/).

## Reopen a recent project

Under the buttons, **Recent** lists up to five recent documents by name, most recent first. Click one to reopen it. Hover over a row to see its full path.

The heading and the list disappear when there's nothing recent. [**File ▸ Open Recent**](/projects/open-a-project/#open-a-recent-project) keeps the same list, so **Clear Menu** empties this one too, the next time the window opens.

## Drop files on it

Drag a file or a project from the Finder and drop it anywhere on the window. Each file opens as its own document, so several files make several projects.

The window takes `.framejob` projects and the movie, sound and picture types **File ▸ Open…** lists, and ignores anything else. The line at the foot of the window names the common ones: MOV · MP4 · M4V · M4A · MP3 · WAV · AIFF · PNG · JPEG · HEIC.

"It isn't an effect you apply to another clip, and it isn't a video or image file. It's transparent wherever it draws nothing, so a lower third on a track above your footage shows the footage around it.\n")

edit('graphics/what-is-a-graphic.mdx',
"It draws a picture, as SVG (a text format for vector drawings), for any frame Frame Job asks for.\n",
"It draws a picture, as SVG (a text format for vector drawings), for any frame Frame Job asks for.\n\n"
"A module is code. It has no keyframes of its own and no expression language: its `render` function works out each frame, and [actions](/graphics/animate-properties/) animate its properties from the timeline. Frame Job can't open a Lottie file or a motion template from another app. **From File…** in the Insert Graphic sheet takes a `.js` module or a `.fjgraphic` package, so to bring an animation across, [write it as a module](/graphics/write-a-module/) or have [an agent](/graphics/agents-and-graphics/) write it.\n")

# --- write a module ---
edit('graphics/write-a-module.mdx',
"A module is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript. It exports `render`, and optionally `meta` and `schema`.\n",
"A module is one file of plain JavaScript, not TypeScript or JSX. It exports `render`, and optionally `meta` and `schema`. To write in TypeScript, compile to a single `.js` file first. [`API.d.ts`](/graphics/edit-a-module/#apimd-and-apidts) has the types for your editor.\n")

edit('graphics/write-a-module.mdx',
"Trim its front, or split it, and the later clip starts at a later frame, so the graphic carries on instead of restarting.\n",
"Trim its front, or split it, and the later clip starts at a later frame, so the graphic carries on instead of restarting.\n\n"
"Work out each frame from `frame` alone. Frames aren't drawn in order and a module can be loaded more than once, so a variable at the top level can't carry anything from one frame to the next. Keep the top level for constants.\n")

edit('graphics/write-a-module.mdx',
"Gradients are dithered so that dark ones don't band.\n",
"Gradients are dithered so that dark ones don't band.\n\n"
"Anything you don't draw is transparent, so the tracks behind the clip show through. To fill the frame with a colour, pass `background` to [`svg()`](/graphics/module-api/#svg).\n\n"
"Most of SVG works, not only shapes, paths and text:\n\n"
"- Gradients, patterns, `<clipPath>`, `<mask>`, `<marker>`, `<use>`, `<symbol>` and `<textPath>`.\n"
"- Filters, such as `feGaussianBlur`, `feDropShadow` and `feColorMatrix`.\n"
"- `opacity` and `mix-blend-mode`. These work inside the graphic's own picture. To blend with the tracks behind it, use the clip's [blend mode](/canvas/blend-modes/).\n"
"- `<style>` sheets and `style` attributes.\n\n"
"Each frame is one still picture, so `<animate>`, `<animateTransform>` and CSS animations do nothing. Change what `render` returns instead. `<foreignObject>`, which is how HTML gets into an SVG, doesn't draw either, and neither does `<script>`. None of these gives a warning.\n")

edit('graphics/write-a-module.mdx',
"There's also no `fetch`, no file access, no clock, no `performance`, no `WebAssembly` and no `Intl`. For numbers with thousands separators, use `formatNumber`.\n",
"There's also no `fetch`, no file access, no clock, no `performance`, no `WebAssembly` and no `Intl`. For numbers with thousands separators, use `formatNumber`.\n\n"
"It isn't a browser or Node either. There's no `document`, `window`, `<canvas>` or WebGL, and no `setTimeout` or `requestAnimationFrame`. There's no `console`, so `console.log` stops the frame with `ReferenceError: console is not defined`. See [Debug a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/#debug-a-module) for what to do instead. `render` can't be `async`, because nothing waits for a promise.\n\n"
"You can't install an npm package or import one. Code you paste or bundle into the one file does run, as long as it needs nothing listed here and its top level fits [the time budget](#the-time-budget).\n\n"
"To feed a graphic data, such as a chart's numbers, pass it in a `string` prop and parse it in `render`, or write it into the module.\n")
